intro: Fourteen centuries ago, Justinian's architects set a 31-meter dome on pendentives and changed architecture forever. This is the story of the great church that became a mosque, a museum, and a movie star.
page_title: Hagia Sophia: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: After the Nika riots of 532 burned the earlier basilica, Emperor Justinian I ordered a church to outdo Solomon's Temple; entering it he is said to have declared, Solomon, I have outdone you. His architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus raised it in just five years, 532 to 537. The breakthrough was the pendentive: spherical triangles transitioning from the square bay to the circular dome, letting a 31 m dome crown a rectangular church. Forty windows ring the dome's base, and their light makes the vast shell appear to float.
sections.heading: A dome on pendentives

sections.body: The church is 82 m long and 73 m wide, with two great semi-domes bracing the central dome east and west, 107 columns, and galleries above the aisles. For nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral in the world and the coronation church of Byzantine emperors. When Ottoman Turks took Constantinople in 1453 it became a mosque; four minarets were added, and it became the model for the Blue Mosque next door. It served as a museum from 1935.
sections.heading: Church, mosque, museum

sections.body:
Istanbul is Bond country. The city was Ian Fleming's favorite, and Hagia Sophia appears in two Bond films. In From Russia with Love (1963), Sean Connery's Bond is chased on foot through the building itself, in sequences shot within Hagia Sophia and the nearby Basilica Cistern that rank among the series' most memorable location moments. Nearly fifty years later, Skyfall (2012) returned to Istanbul for its opening, with the 1,500-year-old building glimpsed as Bond races through the city. The World Is Not Enough (1999) also used Istanbul, centering on the Maiden's Tower.

The building's screen career fits its history: for fourteen centuries it has been the backdrop against which empires performed, from Byzantine coronations to Ottoman prayers to a spy running for his life.
